headline.headline: TIGERS MAUL PHILLIES 10-2 AS DETROIT ERUPTS FOR EIGHT RUNS IN FINAL TWO INNINGS
headline.deck: Hill, McGonigle homer as Detroit's bats explode late at Comerica Park
headline.body:
DETROIT -- The Philadelphia Phillies arrived at Comerica Park and left in ruins Friday night, dismantled 10-2 by the Detroit Tigers in a game that turned savage in the sixth inning and never looked back. What had been a tense, low-scoring affair through five innings became a rout when Detroit sent seven batters across the plate over the sixth and seventh frames, blowing the game wide open before 34,084 fans.

The Tigers received home run contributions from Hill, who connected for his seventh of the season, and McGonigle, whose eighth long ball of the year added to the carnage. Jack Flaherty, on the mound for Detroit, also hit Alec Bohm with a pitch, but the Phillies could muster nothing in response -- blanked in six of nine innings and held to a single run in the third and one more in the fourth. The visitors were finished long before the final out.

The game took just 2 hours and 32 minutes to complete, a brisk finish given the final margin. Detroit's sixth-inning eruption of five runs proved the knockout blow, with three more added in the seventh for good measure. The Phillies, who managed just two runs on the night, saw their bats go entirely silent from the fifth inning onward as Detroit's pitching and defense combined to salt the game away.

secondary.headline: YANKEES RALLY IN NINTH TO OUTLAST NATIONALS 5-3
secondary.deck: New York scores three in ninth after two-hour rain delay tests both clubs
secondary.body:
WASHINGTON -- The New York Yankees refused to go quietly Friday, scoring three runs in the top of the ninth inning to pull away from the Washington Nationals 5-3 in a game stretched to 3 hours and 6 minutes by a two-hour weather delay. Clayton Beeter earned the win for New York in a contest that saw the Nationals pull within one run at 2-1 after the third inning, only to watch the Yankees regain control late.

The Yankees led 2-0 after the first inning, then watched Washington tie things with a run in the third before New York added another in the fourth to push ahead 3-1. The Nationals surged back in the seventh with two runs to make it a 3-3 game, but New York's three-run ninth off Washington's bullpen settled matters. Attendance at Nationals Park was 38,085, a strong crowd that endured the lengthy delay to see the finish.

secondary.headline: REDS SHUT OUT CUBS 4-0 BEHIND CRUZ, BLEDAY HOMERS
secondary.deck: Cincinnati blanks Chicago as Nelson Cruz and J.D. Bleday each reach 15 home runs
secondary.body:
CINCINNATI -- The Cincinnati Reds needed just one swing of momentum to put the Chicago Cubs away Friday, and they found it in the fifth and seventh innings at Great American Ball Park. Nelson Cruz hit his 15th home run of the season and Jo Adell Bleday matched him with his own 15th as the Reds rolled to a 4-0 shutout victory before 30,878 fans.

Cruz also contributed a triple and went extra bases twice on the night, while Seiya Suzuki provided one of Chicago's few bright moments with a double. The Cubs left 12 runners on base, a damning total that illustrated how thoroughly Cincinnati's pitching suffocated any Cub scoring threat. The Reds scored once in the fifth and added three more in the seventh to close out the shutout, finishing the game in 2 hours and 35 minutes.

secondary.headline: CAMINERO'S 28TH HOMER POWERS RAYS PAST MARINERS 7-2
secondary.deck: Tampa Bay's young slugger stays red-hot as Rays roll at Tropicana Field
secondary.body:
ST. PETERSBURG -- Junior Caminero showed no signs of slowing down Friday, drilling his 28th home run of the season to lead the Tampa Bay Rays to a 7-2 victory over the Seattle Mariners at Tropicana Field. The 22-year-old's blast highlighted a decisive seventh-inning rally in which the Rays plated three runs to break open a close game, finishing off Seattle before a modest crowd of 15,568.

Tampa Bay had led 2-1 through six innings before the seventh-inning surge put the game out of reach. Colby Mullins also homered for the Rays, connecting for his 11th of the year, while Young added his 11th as well. Seattle's Mullin answered with an 11th-inning homer but could not generate enough offense, with the Mariners scoring once in the fifth and once in the sixth before going quiet. The game was completed in a crisp 2 hours and 22 minutes.

column.headline: DETROIT'S LATE-INNING THUNDER IS THE REAL STORY OF JULY
column.body:
Eight runs in two innings against a Phillies club that arrived in Detroit with postseason ambitions -- that is not a coincidence. That is a lineup announcing itself. The Tigers have the kind of middle-of-the-order pop, evidenced by Hill and McGonigle going deep on the same night, that makes them dangerous in the American League in a way that standings alone do not fully capture. When a team scores five in the sixth and three in the seventh against a respectable pitching staff, that is something worth circling on the calendar.

The Phillies have the talent to bounce back, but walking out of Comerica Park having scored just two runs -- both arriving before the fifth inning -- is a reminder that Philadelphia's offense cannot be taken for granted any more than Detroit's can be dismissed. The Tigers are playing like a club that has found something. The rest of the AL should be paying close attention.

story.headline: WHITE SOX CRUSH ATHLETICS 14-1 AS VARGAS, PETERS POWER SEVEN-RUN SEVENTH
story.deck: Chicago erupts for eight runs in one frame to end the Athletics' misery
story.body:
CHICAGO — The Chicago White Sox turned a quiet afternoon into a rout Friday, blasting the Athletics 14-1 at Guaranteed Rate Field behind a savage seven-run seventh inning that put the game beyond any reasonable doubt. Oscar Vargas, who collected a double and his 21st home run of the season, and Jake Peters, who launched his sixth homer and added a triple and a double, led the destruction as the Sox piled up 14 runs on a day the Athletics never found their footing.

The game was scoreless through four innings before Chicago opened the scoring with four runs in the fifth. The Athletics managed just a single run in the seventh, long after the damage was done. Vargas finished with multiple extra-base hits, and Peters had himself one of the more complete offensive performances of any player in the American League this week, reaching base multiple times and doing damage at every turn. A hit-by-pitch on Bolte, issued by Burke S., was the closest thing to A's offense for most of the afternoon.

The final attendance of 37,539 at home saw the White Sox send 14 men across the plate while limiting the Athletics to one measly run on eight runners left on base. Chicago also got doubles from Murakami, Meidroth, and Benintendi, while Antonacci added a stolen base. The Athletics, who stranded eight baserunners, will look to avoid further embarrassment as the series continues.

story.headline: WILSON ERUPTS FOR 35 IN BULLS DEBUT, SECOND-BEST VEGAS OPENING EVER
story.deck: Chicago's prized rookie Caleb Wilson announces himself with a historic Las Vegas performance.
story.body:
LAS VEGAS -- Caleb Wilson did not ease into professional basketball. The Chicago Bulls rookie exploded for 35 points Friday night in his summer league debut at the Thomas & Mack Center, a performance that left scouts, coaches and opposing defenders shaking their heads in disbelief. The total stands as the second-highest scoring debut in Las Vegas Summer League history, a record book that stretches back more than two decades of hopeful prospects chasing their NBA dreams under the desert lights.

Wilson, who was visibly overwhelmed by the moment after the final buzzer, described the night as deeply personal. The Bulls rookie drained jumpers from the mid-range, attacked the rim with force and knocked down shots from beyond the arc with the kind of confidence that teams spend lottery picks hoping to find. Chicago's front office, which made Wilson a centerpiece of its rebuilding effort, watched from the stands as their investment announced itself to the entire league in stunning fashion.

The performance overshadowed a full slate of summer league action that included matchups featuring the Portland Trail Blazers against the Phoenix Suns, Oklahoma City Thunder against the Los Angeles Lakers, Boston Celtics against the Toronto Raptors, and Chicago's own contest against the Memphis Grizzlies. But no box score from the day generated the electricity that Wilson's 35-point statement produced. The Bulls, starved for a transcendent talent to anchor their rebuild, may have found exactly what they were looking for.

story.headline: DUCKS MATCH RECORD $90M OFFER SHEET TO KEEP CARLSSON, LEAFS PURGE FRONT OFFICE IN TURBULENT NHL OFFSEASON
story.deck: Anaheim retains its 21-year-old star center while Toronto shakes up its front office.
story.body:
The Anaheim Ducks blinked first in the NHL's most dramatic offer sheet saga in years, announcing Saturday they will match the Philadelphia Flyers' stunning five-year, $90 million contract tendered to star center Leo Carlsson, locking up the 21-year-old Swede at $18 million annually through the prime of his career. The deal sets an NHL record and signals just how desperately both franchises coveted Carlsson, who emerged last season as one of the most gifted young pivots in the league. The Flyers, who fired the opening shot by submitting the offer sheet, will walk away empty-handed but forced Anaheim to commit historic money to a player who has yet to reach his peak.

Carlsson himself addressed the whirlwind publicly on Saturday, describing the surreal experience of watching two franchises wage financial war over his services. The Norrkoping, Sweden, native said the offer sheet process was unlike anything he had experienced in hockey, and that he is grateful to remain in Anaheim, where he has built relationships with teammates and coaching staff since being selected second overall in the 2023 draft. General manager Pat Verbeek declined to express irritation toward Philadelphia, but the nine-figure commitment leaves Anaheim with precious little cap flexibility heading into a crucial roster-building summer.

Meanwhile, chaos descended upon Toronto as the Maple Leafs fired assistant general manager Hayley Wickenheiser as part of a sweeping front office purge that sent shockwaves through the hockey world. Wickenheiser, a four-time Olympic gold medalist and one of the most celebrated players in the history of women's hockey, had served in the organization since 2018 and was widely regarded as a rising executive. The dismissals signal a dramatic change in direction for a franchise under mounting pressure to finally convert its roster talent into a Stanley Cup championship, with ownership apparently determined to rebuild the decision-making structure from the top down.

story.headline: QUARTERBACK CAROUSEL SPINS WILDLY AS TEAMS RETOOL FOR 2026 CAMPAIGN
story.deck: Several franchises made bold moves this spring to reshape their rosters at the most important position.
story.body:
The NFL offseason has turned into a full-blown quarterback market, with teams scrambling to secure signal-callers before training camps open in late July. The Cleveland Browns, desperate after another dismal showing in the 2025 season, agreed to terms with veteran quarterback Sam Darnold on a two-year deal worth $52 million, betting the former USC product can stabilize a franchise that has cycled through starters for years. Meanwhile, the Las Vegas Raiders swung a blockbuster trade with the Tennessee Titans, shipping three draft picks to land Levis, who struggled in Nashville but whose arm talent remains coveted across the league.

The 2026 NFL Draft in late April added more fuel to the fire. The New England Patriots, holding the second overall pick, selected Ole Miss quarterback Jaxson Dart, drawing immediate comparisons to franchise cornerstones of the Belichick era. Draft analysts praised Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel for landing a polished pocket passer who threw for 4,279 yards last season in the SEC, calling it the shrewdest selection of the first round. The Jacksonville Jaguars, picking fourth, pivoted to defense and grabbed edge rusher James Pearce Jr. out of Tennessee to bolster a pass rush that ranked near the bottom of the league in sacks in 2025.

Beyond the quarterback moves, the offseason has been defined by veteran reshuffling across contenders. The Philadelphia Eagles, fresh off their Super Bowl LX title run, locked up wide receiver DeVonta Smith on a three-year extension worth $87 million, ensuring Jalen Hurts retains his most reliable target heading into the new season. The San Francisco 49ers, meanwhile, released aging linebacker Fred Warner in a cost-cutting move that stunned the Bay Area fan base, signaling a genuine roster rebuild under general manager John Lynch. Training camps cannot open soon enough for a league buzzing with change.
